subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 10 periods = 500 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 8h 20min

periods.activity_title: Propositions, Converses and the Meaning of Truth

textbook_items_in_class.description: Proposition P 'If it rains, then the road is wet' and its converse Q 'If the road is wet, then it has rained': P is true but Q may not be, introducing a counterexample.

time_bands.activity: Open by writing two statements on the board: 'If two sides of a triangle are equal, then the angles opposite the equal sides are equal' and 'If two angles of a triangle are equal, then the sides opposite the equal angles have equal lengths.' Ask students which of these comes first logically and whether knowing one is true tells us anything about the other. Collect two or three responses without judgment, then introduce the vocabulary: a proposition is a statement that is either true or false, and the second statement is the converse of the first because it swaps the 'if' and 'then' parts.

Write the general form 'If X then Y' on the board and show that its converse is 'If Y then X.' Introduce the interchangeable form 'X implies Y.' Work through Example 1, p.1 together: the proposition 'If it rains, then the road is wet' is true, but the converse 'If the road is wet, then it has rained' can fail — a tanker may have spilled water. Establish formally that a situation showing a proposition is false is called a counterexample, stressing that one good counterexample settles the matter. Mention Fermat's claim about numbers of the form 2^(2^n) + 1 and how Euler found a single counterexample to refute it — making the historical point that counterexamples are a key tool in mathematics.

Students individually write the converse of each of the following propositions on their notebooks: (a) 'If a shape is a square, it has four equal sides.' (b) 'If it is noon, the sun is overhead.' For each, they write one sentence saying whether the converse appears true or false, and if false, a counterexample. Pairs then compare and discuss. Take two examples from the class and discuss on the board.

Close by asking: can a proposition be true while its converse is false? Can both be true? Can both be false? Take brief oral responses. Write the three possibilities on the board as an open question the class will explore in upcoming units, leaving the third case as a puzzle. Assign homework.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the chapter's entry point: the two triangle statements at the opening are the chapter's own motivating pair, and returning to them at the close gives continuity without requiring anything to have been taught before. A common error here is treating 'the converse is false' as meaning 'the proposition is false' — watch for students who conflate the truth of a statement with the truth of its converse. Example 3, p.2 (perfect squares and factor counts) is a rich self-study item students may read to see another early instance of the proposition–converse question.
homework: Write the converse of Exercise Set 9.1 Q1, p.5 (parallel lines and corresponding angles). State whether the original proposition is true or false, and whether the converse is true or false, in one sentence each — no justification needed yet.

periods.activity_title: Justifying True Propositions and Finding Counterexamples

textbook_items_in_class.description: Multiples of 6 are always multiples of 3 (true); converse that every multiple of 3 is a multiple of 6 (false, with counterexample).
Converse of parallel lines and corresponding angles proposition; truth or falsity with justification or counterexample.
Converse of 'a quadrilateral is a square implies all its angles are equal'; truth or falsity with justification or counterexample.

time_bands.activity: Work through Example 2, p.2 as a class demonstration. Write the proposition 'If a number is a multiple of 6, then it is a multiple of 3' and ask a student to explain in words why it must be true (every multiple of 6 is 6k = 2 × 3k, which is clearly a multiple of 3). Write a brief two-line justification on the board. Then ask: is the converse true? Invite a quick counterexample — 9 is a multiple of 3 but not of 6. Emphasise that the justification for the true direction is a short deductive argument, not just several examples.

Students work in pairs on Exercise Set 9.1 Q1, p.5 and Q2, p.5. For each, they must: (1) write the converse explicitly, (2) state whether the original is true or false with a brief reason or counterexample, (3) state whether the converse is true or false with a brief reason or counterexample. Circulate and prompt pairs who write only examples instead of a general justification for the true direction.

Select two pairs to present Q1 and Q2 respectively on the board. For Q1, the class checks: is the justification for the true statement a general argument or just an example? For Q2, check that the counterexample for the converse actually contradicts the converse, not the original. Discuss briefly what makes a counterexample valid.

Quick oral check: teacher states a proposition (e.g. 'If a number ends in 0, it is divisible by 5'). Students write the converse on their notebooks in 60 seconds. Two students read aloud. Close by naming the two skills this unit has practised: constructing a brief deductive justification and finding a counterexample.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the vocabulary established around propositions and converses, this unit shifts the work toward the student producing both justifications and counterexamples independently. A frequent error is offering a collection of examples as a justification for a true proposition — reinforce that a general deductive argument (even a short one) is required. For a self-study pointer, Exercise Set 9.1 Q4, p.6 extends the same skills to an algebraic setting the student can work through independently.
homework: Complete Exercise Set 9.1 Q4, p.6 independently: write the converse, decide whether each is true, and justify or give a counterexample.

periods.activity_title: Factor-Partner Pairs: Proving Propositions in Both Directions

textbook_items_in_class.description: Perfect squares and an odd number of factors: factor-partner argument proves both the proposition P and its converse Q, so the two statements imply each other.

time_bands.activity: Write the two statements on the board: P — 'If n is a perfect square, then it has an odd number of factors'; Q — 'If n has an odd number of factors, then it is a perfect square.' Ask students to check both for n = 36, n = 12, and n = 25 by listing all factors. Students do this in notebooks while the teacher circulates. Brief oral share: for which n did P hold? For which did Q hold?

Work through the factor-partner Discussion from Example 3, p.2 step by step on the board. Every factor f of n has a partner f' such that f × f' = n, illustrated with (1,12), (2,6), (3,4) for 12 and (1,36), (2,18), (3,12), (4,9), (6,6) for 36. Reason through the chain: 'n has an odd number of factors' implies there is a self-partnering factor f with f × f = n, which means n = f² is a perfect square. Ask students aloud: does this chain prove P or Q? Take responses — it proves Q because it starts from 'odd number of factors.' Then modify: starting from n = f², the self-partner (f, f) exists, but does that immediately make the total count odd? Reason carefully that a number cannot have two distinct self-partnering factors (since f × f = g × g = n would force f = g), so exactly one self-partnering pair exists, making the total count odd — this proves P.

Students independently write up, in their notebooks, the two-direction argument in their own words: first Q (from odd factors to perfect square), then P (from perfect square to odd factors). They must name, for each direction, the step that closes the argument. Teacher selects two notebooks to read aloud, correcting any logical gap.

Discussion prompt from Think and Reflect: 'Can both a proposition and its converse be false? Think of an example.' Students jot a response. Take one or two contributions — the class does not need to reach a final answer yet; the purpose is to open up the third case alongside the ones already seen (one true/one false; both true).

periods.teacher_notes: The key difficulty here is that students often accept the factor-partner argument as proving both directions simultaneously, without seeing that it is a chain in one direction only. Insist that students name the starting assumption for each direction. A common error is claiming that 'n has two self-partnering factors, e.g. (2,2) and (3,3), giving an even count' — work through why this is impossible: if f² = n and g² = n, then f² = g² forces f = g for positive integers. Exercise Set 9.1 Q9, p.6 (square of a prime has exactly three factors) is a natural self-study extension.
homework: Exercise Set 9.1 Q5, p.6: frame the converse of 'If a and b are perfect squares, then ab is a perfect square', decide whether each is true, and justify or give a counterexample.

periods.activity_title: Area, Congruence and the Four Possible Relationships

textbook_items_in_class.description: Proposition 'If two triangles have the same area, then they are congruent' (false) and converse 'If two triangles are congruent, then they have the same area' (true): justification and counterexample.
Converse of 'If x = y, then a + x = a + y'; truth of each direction with justification or counterexample.

time_bands.activity: Pose Example 4, p.3 as a challenge: students work individually to decide whether P ('same area implies congruent') and Q ('congruent implies same area') are true or false, writing one sentence of justification or a counterexample for each. After five minutes of individual work, pairs compare. Then the class discusses: for Q, students should produce the standard argument that congruent triangles have identical side lengths, so their areas computed by ½ × base × height must agree. For P, a right triangle with legs 3, 4 (area 6) and a right triangle with legs 2, 6 (area 6) are not congruent — make this concrete on the board.

Summarise on the board the three cases now established: (i) a true proposition with a false converse (rain/road, multiples of 3 and 6); (ii) both proposition and converse true (perfect squares and odd factor count). Then return to the Think and Reflect observation from the section: both can also be false. Ask students to attempt this: can they write a proposition of the form 'If X then Y' where both P and Q are false? Give them three minutes individually, then share. Guide if needed: 'If a number is odd, then it is prime' is false (9 is odd but not prime); its converse 'If a number is prime, then it is odd' is also false (2 is prime but not odd).

Students work on Exercise Set 9.1 Q4, p.6 in pairs. They write the converse of 'If x = y, then a + x = a + y', decide whether each direction is true, and write a brief justification for the true direction. Circulate and note any pair who confuses the direction of the subtraction argument. Bring the class together: the forward direction follows from the additive property; the converse follows by subtracting a from both sides — both are true, making this a case of mutual implication.

Ask students to write, in one compact table in their notebooks, the four logical cases: (1) P true, Q false; (2) P false, Q true; (3) both true; (4) both false — with one example of each from what they have now seen in class. Collect notebooks briefly to check, or ask pairs to read their tables aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that factor-partner reasoning can make both directions true, this unit introduces the third and fourth possibilities explicitly. The most common error with Example 4, p.3 is that students accept 'same area' as sufficient for congruence because they only think of triangles with the same shape — a prompt to draw two clearly different triangles with the same base and height usually dispels this. For a self-study pointer, Exercise Set 9.1 Q5, p.6 (perfect squares and their products) offers a clean pair to classify independently.
homework: Exercise Set 9.1 Q6, p.6 and Q7, p.6: for each, write the converse, decide whether each statement is true or false, and justify or give a counterexample in two to three lines.

periods.activity_title: Proving the Converse of the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras Theorem

textbook_items_in_class.description: States the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem, forms its converse, and proves the converse using construction of a right triangle and the SSS criterion.

time_bands.activity: Write the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem on the board in the chapter's two-sentence form: 'Let a, b, c be the side lengths of a triangle. If the triangle is right-angled, then a² + b² = c².' Ask a student to frame the converse by keeping the first sentence and changing the second. Write the converse the class produces: 'If a² + b² = c², then the triangle is right-angled.' Pose the question for the unit: is this converse true? Students write a one-sentence conjecture in their notebooks.

Lead the proof of the converse from Example 5, p.4, step by step, on the board. Given ∆ABC with side lengths a, b, c and a² + b² = c², construct a right triangle ∆XYZ with the right angle at Z, perpendicular sides YZ = a and XZ = b. Apply the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem to ∆XYZ (which is right-angled by construction) to obtain XY² = a² + b² = c², so XY = c. Now ∆ABC and ∆XYZ have all three sides equal (a, b, c), so by the SSS congruence criterion they are congruent. Since ∆XYZ is right-angled at Z, ∆ABC must also have a right angle at the corresponding vertex. Pause after each step and ask: why is this step valid? Students note each step in their notebooks with a one-line reason.

Students write up the proof in their own words, in full sentences, without looking at the board (board can be wiped after the group reconstruction). Emphasise: the proof must name (i) what is given, (ii) what is constructed and why, (iii) how SSS is applied, and (iv) the conclusion. Pairs exchange notebooks and check each other's proof for missing steps.

Brief reflection: why did the proof need to construct a separate right triangle rather than working directly with ∆ABC? Take one or two responses. Establish that the construction creates an object with a known right angle that can then be compared to ∆ABC — a technique of indirect construction used in deductive proofs.

periods.teacher_notes: The Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem itself is treated as a known result here; the unit's purpose is the proof of its converse by construction and SSS. A common error is applying the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem directly to ∆ABC (which is what needs to be proved right-angled) rather than to the freshly constructed ∆XYZ — make this logical order explicit. Exercise Set 9.1 Q16, p.6 (divisibility by 3 and digit sum) is a self-study item that uses the same structure of proving both directions of an equivalence.
homework: In three to four sentences, explain in writing why the proof of the converse of the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem cannot simply apply the theorem directly to ∆ABC. What role does ∆XYZ play?

periods.activity_title: Language Variants of 'If-Then' and Divisibility Propositions

textbook_items_in_class.description: Converse of 'If n is divisible by 24, then it is divisible by both 4 and 6'; truth of each direction.
Converse of 'If n is divisible by 60, then it is divisible by both 5 and 12'; truth of each direction.
Divisibility by 8 versus divisibility by 2 and 4; justify the forward direction and decide whether the converse holds.

time_bands.activity: Revisit the 'Note' from section 9.1 on language variants: write on the board 'If a number is a perfect square, then it has an odd number of factors' and 'A number has an odd number of factors when it is a perfect square.' Ask students whether these say the same thing — take responses. Establish that 'Y when X' is another way to say 'If X then Y.' Give two further examples on the board and ask students to rewrite them using 'when' and then using 'implies.' Stress that the mathematical content is unchanged.

Students work in groups of three on Exercise Set 9.1 Q8, p.6 and Q9, p.6. For Q8: the forward direction (divisible by 24 implies divisible by 4 and 6) is true — students should give a brief divisibility argument; the converse (divisible by 4 and 6 implies divisible by 24) is false — n = 12 is divisible by both 4 and 6 but not by 24. For Q9: similar analysis with 60, 5, and 12. Groups record their reasoning in full sentences.

Work through Exercise Set 9.1 Q15, p.6 together as a class. The forward direction (divisible by 8 implies divisible by 2 and 4) is justified by writing 8k = 2(4k) = 4(2k). The converse question asks whether divisibility by 2 and 4 is enough to ensure divisibility by 8 — it is not, and n = 4 serves as a counterexample. Discuss why this matters for divisibility shortcuts: checking two simpler conditions does not always substitute for checking the original.

Rapid-fire oral practice: teacher states a proposition about divisibility (e.g. 'If n is divisible by 15, then it is divisible by 3 and 5'); students write the converse and a quick true/false verdict with one word of justification in 90 seconds. Two students share. Close by naming the pattern: the forward direction from a larger divisor to its parts is usually true; the converse rarely is unless the parts together force the larger divisor.

periods.teacher_notes: The Note on language variants is short but important — students will meet 'Y when X' and 'X implies Y' in later chapters and in mathematical writing generally, and confusing the sentence structure with the direction of implication is a persistent error. In Q8 and Q9, watch for groups who test only one value and declare the converse true; insist on a general argument or a genuine counterexample. Exercise Set 9.1 Q11, p.6 (n and n+3 sharing no factors) offers a more subtle divisibility example for students who want additional challenge.
homework: Exercise Set 9.1 Q10, p.6 and Q11, p.6: for each, write the converse, classify the truth of each direction, and provide a brief justification or counterexample.

periods.activity_title: Algebraic Propositions: Squaring, Cubing and Equality

textbook_items_in_class.description: Converse of 'If x = y, then x² = y²' for real x, y; truth of each direction with justification or counterexample.
Converse of 'If x = y, then x³ = y³' for real x, y; truth of each direction with justification or counterexample.
Converse of 'If a and b are perfect squares, then ab is a perfect square'; truth of each direction.

time_bands.activity: Write on the board: 'If x = y, then x² = y²' where x and y are real numbers. Ask students to frame the converse. Students write it in notebooks. Then ask: is the original true? (Yes — squaring both sides of an equality preserves equality.) Is the converse true? Give students two minutes to think and write before sharing. Guide: x = 3 and y = −3 give x² = y² = 9 but x ≠ y — a clean counterexample. Write the counterexample formally.

Students work in pairs on Exercise Set 9.1 Q7, p.6: the proposition 'If x = y, then x³ = y³' and its converse. Forward: true (cubing preserves equality). Converse: 'If x³ = y³, then x = y' — ask pairs to decide. This converse is in fact true for real numbers because the function t ↦ t³ is strictly monotone (if x ≠ y then x³ ≠ y³). Students should argue: if x³ = y³ then x³ − y³ = 0, so (x − y)(x² + xy + y²) = 0, and since x² + xy + y² > 0 for real x, y not both zero... guide the class toward the conclusion that x = y. Contrast with the squaring case.

Students work individually on Exercise Set 9.1 Q5, p.6. They frame the converse of 'If a and b are perfect squares, then ab is a perfect square', determine the truth of each direction, and write full justifications. For the forward direction: a = m², b = n² gives ab = (mn)² — perfect square. For the converse: if ab is a perfect square, must a and b each be? Counterexample: a = 2, b = 8; ab = 16 is a perfect square but neither a nor b is. Circulate and check that students give a fully written counterexample rather than a bare assertion.

Class debrief: compare squaring (where the converse fails) with cubing (where it holds) side by side. Why the difference? Elicit: squaring collapses sign information (x and −x have the same square); cubing does not. Connect to the general principle that an operation's invertibility on its domain determines whether the converse of an implication through that operation is true.

periods.teacher_notes: The contrast between the squaring and cubing cases is mathematically significant: the forward implication is true in both, but only cubing preserves enough information to make the converse true. A common error is claiming the converse of the squaring proposition is also true, often by thinking only of positive values; always prompt with x = 3, y = −3. For the cubing converse, students who cannot construct the algebraic factorisation argument may observe numerically that no real cube root has two distinct real values — accept this as partial justification and encourage the algebraic form.
homework: Exercise Set 9.1 Q12, p.6 and Q13, p.6: find counterexamples to the given primality claims, showing all working.

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find counterexamples to claims that all numbers of the form 4n²+1, n²+n+11, and 4^n+3 are prime.
Find counterexamples to 'If n is prime, then 2^n − 1 is prime' and 'If n is even, then 2^n + 1 is prime'.

time_bands.activity: Recall Fermat's claim from the opening of section 9.1: numbers of the form 2^(2^n) + 1 appear prime for n = 0, 1, 2, 3 (giving 3, 5, 17, 257) but Euler showed 2^(2^5) + 1 = 4294967297 = 641 × 6700417 is composite. Write this on the board and ask: how do you find a counterexample to a 'for all n' claim? Establish the strategy: test small values systematically, and when one fails, you are done.

Groups of three take one formula each from Exercise Set 9.1 Q13, p.6: (i) 4n²+1, (ii) n²+n+11, (iii) 4^n+3. Each group computes values for n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, ... checking each for primality by testing divisibility by small primes, until they find a composite value. Groups record: the formula, the value of n, the resulting number, and its factorisation. Note: for (i), n = 5 gives 4(25)+1 = 101 (prime); n = 10 gives 401 (prime); students may need guidance that n = 0 gives 1, which is not prime — discuss whether 1 counts. For (ii), n = 10 gives 121 = 11². For (iii), n = 1 gives 7 (prime), n = 2 gives 19 (prime), but n = 4 gives 259 = 7 × 37. Groups report.

Work through Exercise Set 9.1 Q14, p.6 as a class. For 'If n is prime, then 2^n − 1 is prime': test n = 2 (3, prime), n = 3 (7, prime), n = 5 (31, prime), n = 11 (2047 = 23 × 89, composite) — counterexample n = 11. For 'If n is even, then 2^n + 1 is prime': n = 2 gives 5 (prime), n = 4 gives 17 (prime), n = 6 gives 65 = 5 × 13 — counterexample n = 6. Stress: finding the counterexample requires no proof that the formula never works; one failure suffices.

Reflection: students write one sentence in their notebooks answering 'What is the difference between showing a proposition is false and showing it is true?' Take two oral responses. Key idea: false requires only one counterexample; true requires a general argument.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit highlights the asymmetry between proving and disproving: a single counterexample refutes a universal claim, but no finite list of examples establishes one. Watch for groups who declare a formula 'works' after five prime values — remind them that Fermat's formula gave four primes before failing. For n²+n+11, guide groups to try n = 10 if they are stuck; the result 121 = 11² is a satisfying surprise. Exercise Set 9.1 Q15, p.6 (divisibility by 8 versus 2 and 4) revisits the asymmetry in a divisibility context.
homework: Exercise Set 9.1 Q16, p.6: express the relationship between 'a number is divisible by 3' and 'sum of its digits is a multiple of 3' using two If-then sentences, and state whether each is true.

periods.activity_title: Propositions About Number of Factors and Divisors

textbook_items_in_class.description: Converse of 'If n is the square of a prime, then it has exactly 3 factors'; truth of each direction.
Converse of 'If n is a product of two unequal primes, then it has exactly 4 divisors'; truth of each direction.
Converse of 'If n and n+3 have no common factors, then n is not a multiple of 3'; truth of each direction.

time_bands.activity: Write on the board: 'If n is the square of a prime, then it has exactly 3 factors.' Ask students to list the factors of p² for p = 2, 3, 5 (giving 1, p, p²) and confirm the proposition for these cases. Then frame the converse: 'If n has exactly 3 factors, then n is the square of a prime.' Ask: could a non-square-of-prime have exactly 3 factors? Students think individually for two minutes. Guide: any integer with exactly 3 factors must have factors 1, d, d² (since the factor list 1, d, n forces n = d²), so d must be prime. Both directions are true — this is a case of mutual implication.

Students work in pairs on Exercise Set 9.1 Q11, p.6: 'If n is a product of two unequal primes p and q, then it has exactly 4 divisors.' Pairs list the divisors of pq (which are 1, p, q, pq) and confirm the forward direction. They frame the converse and decide: is every number with exactly 4 divisors a product of two unequal primes? Guide: consider n = p³; its divisors are 1, p, p², p³ — that is four, but n is not a product of two unequal primes. Counterexample: n = 8 (divisors: 1, 2, 4, 8). Converse is false.

Class works through Exercise Set 9.1 Q12, p.6 together. Proposition: 'If n and n+3 have no common factors, then n is not a multiple of 3.' Forward: if n = 3k, then 3 divides both n and n+3, so they share the factor 3, contradicting the hypothesis — the proposition is true by contrapositive reasoning. Converse: 'If n is not a multiple of 3, then n and n+3 have no common factors.' This requires more care — lead students to check whether any prime p could divide both n and n+3, which forces p | 3, so p = 3, but then p | n, contradicting the hypothesis. Converse is also true.

Students record in notebooks a compact summary of Q10, Q11, Q12: for each, the proposition, its converse, and the truth status of each with one-line reason. Teacher circulates and marks any case where the student has not named the logical structure of their justification (e.g. 'by contrapositive' for Q12 forward).

periods.teacher_notes: Exercises Q10 and Q12 both yield mutual implication — a useful counterbalance to the many cases where only one direction is true. A common error in Q11 is overlooking n = p³ as a four-divisor number, so push students to think beyond the product-of-two-primes template. In Q12, the contrapositive structure deserves explicit naming: 'to prove If A then B, we assume Not-B and derive Not-A' — this is likely students' first conscious encounter with contrapositive reasoning, and articulating it is valuable.
homework: Exercise Set 9.1 Q17, p.7 (parts i and ii): work through both questions about quadrilateral type Q and write full answers in three to four sentences each.

periods.activity_title: Quadrilateral Diagonals and Consolidation Across the Chapter

textbook_items_in_class.description: Quadrilateral type Q constructed from two sticks as diagonals: decide, for each of two versions of the proposition about equal diagonals, whether the sticks must be equal in length and whether arrangement matters.
Express the relationship between divisibility by 3 and digit-sum divisibility using If-then sentences.

time_bands.activity: Students work in pairs on Exercise Set 9.1 Q17, p.7. Part (i): Q satisfies 'If a quadrilateral is of type Q, then it has equal-length diagonals.' Students answer (a): must the two sticks be equal in length? (Yes — the sticks are the diagonals, so equal diagonals means equal sticks.) And (b): does it matter how the sticks are placed? (No — the length condition does not constrain where they cross or the angle between them.) Part (ii): Q now satisfies 'If a quadrilateral has equal diagonals, then it is of type Q.' Students answer (a) and (b) for this version. In part (ii), for a quadrilateral to qualify as type Q it needs equal diagonals — same stick-length requirement — but now the converse puts the equal-diagonal condition on the hypothesis, meaning any equal-diagonal quadrilateral must be of type Q, so arrangement still does not affect length but may affect other properties. Students write full answers.

Pairs share answers to Q17. Facilitate a class discussion on how swapping which side of the proposition carries the condition changes what the construction must guarantee. Then work through Exercise Set 9.1 Q16, p.6 quickly: students write both If-then sentences expressing the divisibility-by-3 / digit-sum equivalence and confirm both are true.

Chapter consolidation: teacher writes on the board a set of five propositions drawn from across the chapter (one from divisibility, one from geometry, one from number of factors, one algebraic, one about primality). Students classify each as: (A) true proposition, false converse; (B) both true; (C) both false; (D) false proposition, true converse. For each, they write one sentence of justification or give a counterexample. This is done individually, then pairs compare.

Class debrief on the consolidation exercise. Discuss any case where pairs disagreed and reason through it together. Close by articulating the chapter's central discipline: for any proposition of the form 'If X then Y', mathematics demands that you decide independently whether P and its converse Q are true, produce a deductive argument for the true ones, and a specific counterexample for the false ones. Students write this as a one-sentence summary in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Exercise Q17 is a rich geometric reasoning task: the key insight is that the two versions of the proposition (Q has equal diagonals vs any equal-diagonal quad is Q) impose different logical constraints on what the construction must satisfy. A common error is treating both parts of Q17 as equivalent because 'equal diagonals' appears in both — the asymmetry of the implication is exactly what distinguishes them. The consolidation activity at the end should revisit the four logical cases the class has encountered across the chapter, reinforcing that position in a chapter does not determine truth.

implied_lo: Students can frame the converse of a proposition stated in 'if X then Y' form and determine whether each is true, justifying true propositions with a deductive argument and refuting false ones with a specific counterexample.
Students can prove a mathematical proposition by constructing a complete deductive argument from definitions and known results, distinguishing what a given argument proves from what it does not.

questions.question_text: Consider the proposition P: 'If a number is divisible by 6, then it is divisible by 3.' Which of the following correctly describes the converse of P and its truth?

options.label: A
options.text: Converse: 'If a number is divisible by 3, then it is divisible by 6.' The converse is false; 9 is divisible by 3 but not by 6.

options.label: B
options.text: Converse: 'If a number is not divisible by 6, then it is not divisible by 3.' The converse is true because the two conditions are equivalent.

options.label: C
options.text: Converse: 'If a number is divisible by 3, then it is divisible by 6.' The converse is true; every multiple of 3 is also a multiple of 6.

options.label: D
options.text: Converse: 'If a number is divisible by 6, then it is divisible by 3.' This is the same as P; a proposition and its converse are always the same statement.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses the converse ('If Y then X') with the contrapositive ('If not-Y then not-X'); also incorrectly claims equivalence between divisibility by 3 and by 6.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Correctly identifies the converse but asserts it is true without checking; overlooks the counterexample n = 9 (or n = 3), which is divisible by 3 but not by 6.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Misunderstands the definition of converse, treating the original and its converse as identical; does not recognise that swapping the 'if' and 'then' parts produces a different — and potentially non-equivalent — statement.

MCQ.inclusivity: A student who finds the abstraction of the general form difficult may be invited to test n = 3, 6, 9, 12 first and then frame the converse from the pattern observed; a student who answers quickly may be challenged to write a second proposition whose converse is also true and to justify both directions.

questions.question_text:
A student writes the following argument and claims it proves both propositions P and Q simultaneously.

P: 'If n is a perfect square, then n has an odd number of factors.'
Q: 'If n has an odd number of factors, then n is a perfect square.'

The student's argument: 'Every factor f of n can be paired with a partner f' such that f × f' = n. If two factors in the same pair are equal — that is, f = f' — then f² = n, so n is a perfect square. A number with an odd total factor count must have at least one self-paired factor, because unequal pairs use up an even number of slots; the one leftover must be self-paired. Therefore n is a perfect square and has an odd number of factors.'

(a) State precisely which of P or Q the student's argument proves, and explain why it does not prove both.
(b) Modify or extend the argument to prove the other proposition, clearly naming the starting assumption and every step.
look_for: Part (a): Correctly identifies that the argument proves Q (starts from 'n has an odd number of factors' and concludes 'n is a perfect square'), not P.
Part (a): Explains the directional structure of the argument — it assumes odd factor count and derives perfect-square property; it does not start from n being a perfect square.
Part (a): Notes that claiming both directions are proved simultaneously conflates Q's proof chain with P's starting point.
Part (b): Begins the proof of P from the assumption that n = f² for some positive integer f (n is a perfect square).
Part (b): Argues that n therefore has a self-paired factor (f, f) with f × f = n.

Part (b): Closes the argument by establishing that n cannot have two distinct self-paired factors (since f² = g² forces f = g for positive integers), so exactly one pair is self-paired, and all other pairs are unequal — making the total factor count odd.
Overall: uses precise logical language distinguishing assumption from conclusion; does not rely on examples as proof.

ECR.inclusivity: A student who struggles to articulate the directional error may be supported by writing the argument as a chain of arrows (A → B → C) and asking 'which arrow goes which way?'; a student who completes both parts fluently may be challenged to write a third proposition whose proof requires identifying exactly where the factor-partner argument must be patched, and to name that patch.
